intro: The Andante sostenuto of the Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68, opens in E major with strings and bassoon, after which the oboe plays a long melody. Near the end, horn and solo violin join the oboe’s melody, and the violin holds its last note across the orchestra’s closing chords.

sections.label: A · Strings, then oboe melody
sections.mNote: Bassoon doubles the opening violin line; an oboe melody follows.

sections.label: B · Off-beat dotted rhythms
sections.mNote: The violins move from E major towards C♯ minor.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme in the winds
sections.mNote: Strings play figuration around the melody; cellos play pizzicato triplets.

sections.label: A′ · Oboe, horn and solo violin
sections.mNote: Oboe, horn and solo violin share the returning oboe melody

sections.label: Coda · Horn theme, solo violin, E major
sections.mNote: The solo violin plays above the closing E-major chords.

cues.title: Opening phrase, strings and bassoon
cues.text: The strings open with a rising and falling line in E major, and a bassoon doubles the violins. Three low horn notes lead into a phrase in a darker harmony.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 1–4, Simrock first edition (1877), p. 27; Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Oboe melody, bars 18–23
cues.text: Most of the strings drop out, and the oboe plays over wind harmony and a light viola accompaniment. Its melody climbs to a high point. Underneath, the strings bring back their opening rise and fall.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 18–23; oboe melody and returning string phrase. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dotted rhythm and turn to C♯ minor
cues.text: After the cadence in E major the violins play a dotted rhythm. Their accents then move off the downbeat into syncopation, and rising semitones lead the harmony towards C♯ minor. The lower strings take over the rhythm at the pace of a funeral march.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 28–38; dotted rhythm, syncopation and turn to C♯ minor. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter from Simrock, 1873
cues.text: On 22 February 1873 the publisher Fritz Simrock wrote to the composer, “Aren’t you doing anything anymore? Am I not to have a symphony from you in ’73 either?” The première took place in November 1876. Hanslick wrote that the musical world had awaited it “with such tense anticipation”.
cues.evidence: Simrock’s letter of 22 February 1873 and Hanslick’s review of the first Vienna performance, both quoted by Marc Mandel in the Boston Symphony programme note; première in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Return of the opening theme, winds
cues.text: At bar 67 oboes and clarinets play the opening theme again, now back in E major. Flutes play above them, the upper strings add a new accompaniment and the cellos play pizzicato triplets below.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 67–71; wind-led reprise and new string accompaniment. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Reactions of Brahms’s friends
cues.text: Brahms’s friends responded to the symphony in different ways. Clara Schumann found the brilliant ending of the finale unconvincing, and Theodor Billroth admired it but objected to the harshness of the first movement. Hermann Levi thought the gentler middle movements belonged in another work.
cues.evidence: The contrasting reactions of Clara Schumann, Theodor Billroth and Hermann Levi are reported by Marc Mandel in the Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Return of the oboe melody
cues.text: The oboe melody returns with horn and solo violin. The violin leaves its section and plays as a soloist for the rest of the movement. The cellos accompany in pizzicato triplets.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 91–100; solo violin, oboe and horn, with pizzicato cello triplets. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, horn and solo violin
cues.text: The horn plays the oboe tune again. Above it the solo violin adds decoration that quickens into sextuplets. The low strings hold E beneath the other parts.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, coda, bars 101–104; horn theme, violin sextuplets and sustained tonic in low strings. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars, solo violin
cues.text: Pizzicato arpeggios rise through the strings to the solo violin, which plays with the bow. Its last note is held over the orchestra’s soft repeated chords. Below it the other strings return to the bow for the final chord.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 123–128; pizzicato arpeggios and solo violin sustained across the final chord repetitions. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: E-major cadence overlaps a dotted phrase
transitions.how: The E-major cadence overlaps with a new dotted phrase in the violins. Second violins and violas echo the phrase while first violins rise by semitones, shifting their accents off the beat. Bassoons and horns join as the phrase grows and moves towards C♯ minor.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 24–38; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Timpani roll before the return
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme in the winds
transitions.how: Strings and winds overlap in four-note groups across the 3/4 bars. The other parts drop out, leaving a soft timpani roll. Oboes and clarinets bring back the opening theme in E major. Flutes harmonise above them, and below them the strings play and the cellos pluck triplets.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 63–71; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Solo violin enters across the cadence
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme in the winds
transitions.to: A′ · Oboe, horn and solo violin
transitions.how: The strings reach a cadence in B major. As the cadence arrives, a solo violin begins the upbeat of the oboe tune. Oboe and horn now share the tune with it, and the harmony moves towards E. Beneath the three soloists the cellos play pizzicato triplets and the other strings play rising figures in reply.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 85–96; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Bass reaches E before the melody
transitions.from: A′ · Oboe, horn and solo violin
transitions.to: Coda · Horn theme, solo violin, E major
transitions.how: In bars 97–104 the bass reaches E, but the upper parts do not complete the cadence. The horn takes the opening of the oboe melody and the solo violin decorates it above. Low strings and second horn hold the tonic. Strings, flutes and timpani continue their off-beat triplets.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 97–104; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: II. Andante sostenuto, pp. 27–34; opening and bars 18, 28, 39, 67, 91, 101 and 123. Bar references follow Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide.

timeline.note: A bassoon doubles the violin melody, and a horn answers within the opening phrase.
The oboe begins a long melody above quiet winds and soft viola notes.
Dotted violin phrases move off the beat as the bass turns towards C♯ minor.
Oboe and clarinet play above off-beat upper strings.
Winds bring back the opening tune above the strings and plucked cello triplets.
Oboe, horn and solo violin share the melody above rising strings and plucked cellos.
The horn plays the oboe melody while the solo violin decorates it with quick figures.
Solo violin holds its last note while winds and strings repeat their closing chords.

composer.epithet: Composer who completed his First Symphony at the age of forty-three and began his Second beside an Austrian lake the following summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853 a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music to them. Robert Schumann heard in him a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen (New Paths). Publishers became interested. Brahms was now expected to fulfil a public prophecy before most of the public had heard any of his music. His piano sonatas were large-scale works. The symphonies Schumann expected took much longer to arrive.

Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob, earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. He studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
